where: the Pairing code field and Approve button, read against the green 'Ready to pair' pill and the 'Rebuild phone search index' button
finding: The read order is inverted. The object the whole screen exists for — a six-character field — is the quietest thing in the frame: it is filled ink-900 on an ink-900 card, so it has no surface of its own and is defined only by a hairline ring, and its button is rendered in disabled grey. Meanwhile the two most emphatic objects both belong to cards that are not the job: the saturated `present` green pill on 'This deployment', and the 'Rebuild phone search index' button, whose label is ink-100 on ink-800 while the primary action directly above it is ink-400 on the same ink-800. Squinting, the page offers a green badge and a maintenance button first; a leader crossing the room from an iPad has to hunt for the field.
evidence: Sampled pixels: the Approve label reads ~ink-400, the Rebuild label ~ink-100, on identical ink-800 fills. The input's background is (15,23,42) — the same value as the card behind it. The only chromatic object above the fold is the green pill at y≈440, on the second card.
direction: Give the pairing field a surface that steps away from its card rather than matching it, and let it be the largest, brightest object on the page. The empty-state primary should not sit in a grey that a secondary button out-brightens — either the secondary utilities step down to a quieter treatment, or the primary keeps its brand fill and reads as waiting rather than refused. And the accent belongs on the path to pairing, not on a config status: the deployment state can be told in ink alone until it is bad.

where: the three sections — 'Pair a kiosk', 'This deployment', 'Phone search' — as a stack
finding: All three are the same object: same rounded-2xl ink-900 card, same ring, same 16px semibold heading, same 14px ink-500 subtitle, same divider, same padding, same 16px gap between them. Nothing in the composition says which one is the screen. The page therefore reads as a three-item settings list that happens to be about kiosks, which is exactly the paragraph-on-the-third-card problem this screen was built to escape. It is worse than neutral for the second and third: 'Phone search' is an index-rebuild utility with no part in pairing, and it is dressed as a peer of the job; 'This deployment' spends a 78px header band, two lines of prose and a divider on a body containing one 20px pill, so the container is emphatically louder than its content.
evidence: Identical `rounded-2xl bg-ink-900 ring-1 ring-ink-800` sections with identical `text-base font-semibold` headers; the page h1 is only one step above them (20px bold vs 16px semibold) while its subtitle is set at the same 14px ink-500 as all three card subtitles. In the fold frame the three card headers at y=134, 371, 502 form one even rhythm with no dominant.
direction: One of these is the screen and two are references. Let the pairing block own the page — full weight, its own scale, ideally not boxed at all but simply the page's content — and let deployment status and the phone-search utility drop to a subordinate register: smaller headings, no equal card chrome, or moved to a side column so they read as margin notes rather than steps. A body containing a single pill does not need a header band and a divider above it.

where: the whole frame with the rail hidden — top bar, page column, and everything below y=422
finding: With the rail gone the page has no left anchor and nothing to hold the frame. The wordmark sits at x=16 in an edge-to-edge bar; the content column is centred and starts at x=112, so the only two structural elements on screen disagree about where left is. Below them a single card floats in a 1440×900 field that is 53% empty vertically and has ~290px of dead margin either side. That is not whitespace, it is an unfinished layout — and the emptiness is doubled up, because the card itself is a 1200px-wide row holding a six-character field. The person this frame is for is the one under the most time pressure, and the composition gives them no focal point at all.
evidence: Last content pixel row is y=422 of 900. Card spans y=168–388, x=112–1328. Header bar is `px-4` full-bleed while the page uses a centred `max-w-7xl px-8` container.
direction: When the rail is absent the page should stop pretending it is a wide app shell. Either bring the column in to a measure that suits its content and centre it optically in the frame — a screen whose entire job is one field can be a centred, generously-scaled focal composition rather than a wide card pinned to the top — or give the bar and the column a shared left edge so the two agree. Do not leave the desktop-width case as the phone layout with the rail deleted.

where: the 'Cannot sign kiosk tokens' pill and the amber panel beneath it, inside 'This deployment'
finding: One condition is stated twice, at two different severities. The pill is `danger` red; the panel restating the same clause four pixels below it is `warn` amber. The reader has to decide which colour is telling the truth, and there is no third state for the two accents to be distinguishing. Compositionally it is also three nested containers deep — card, then amber panel with its own radius and ring, then a code block with a third radius and ring — so the failure notice ends up the loudest and most elaborate object on the page while the pairing field above it, which still works and will still land, has gone silent.
evidence: `bg-danger-500/15 text-danger-400` pill immediately followed by `bg-warn-500/10 text-warn-400 ring-warn-500/25` panel whose first sentence repeats the pill's text verbatim; inside it a `bg-ink-900/60 ring-ink-700` pre.
direction: Pick one accent for this state and let the other job be done by position and size. If the panel carries the explanation, the pill does not need to restate it; if the pill carries the verdict, the panel can drop its own tint and sit as plain body copy with the command block as the only inset. Collapse a level of nesting so the diagnostic is one object, not three boxes inside each other — and keep it visually subordinate to the field, since the note itself says a kiosk showing a code will still pair.

where: the intro paragraph under the h1, the three card subtitles, the field hint, and the trailing paragraph
finding: Five different kinds of sentence — what this screen is, what to do right now, a caveat about what the status does not mean, a note about code lifetime, and end-of-life housekeeping — are set in the same 14px ink-500. Nothing in the type distinguishes the one instruction the reader needs ('open /kiosk, it shows a six-character code') from trivia they will never need ('rebuilds nightly on its own'). The two paragraphs are also run to the full 1152px column, giving lines of roughly 160 characters — a measure nobody finishes, at a moment nobody has time to. The trailing paragraph sits in the same 16px gap that separates the cards, so it reads as an orphaned fourth card with its heading missing.
evidence: `text-sm text-ink-500` on the h1 subtitle, all three h2 subtitles and the closing paragraph; the intro's first line runs from x=256 to x=1366 before wrapping.
direction: Cap prose measure well short of the column so paragraphs wrap at a readable length regardless of how wide the page gets. Then let contrast do hierarchy: the instruction that leads to the field should sit above the ink-500 floor, and the retirement note should sit below it and be clearly separated from the card stack — a larger gap, or a rule — so it stops reading as a section.

where: the Pairing code label, field, hint and Approve button
finding: Two things in this small stack are out of composition. The field is `w-full` — about 1120px of box with mono 0.2em tracking for a value that can never exceed six characters, so its size lies about its content and the caret lands a thousand pixels from where the eye finishes the instruction. And the hint sits between the field and its button: label→field is 4px, field→hint is 4px, hint→button is 12px, so a line of 12px ink-500 trivia is wedged into the one place the reader's hand is moving through.
evidence: `maxlength="6"` on a `w-full ... font-mono tracking-[0.2em]` input; form gap-3 with an inner `gap-1.5 pointer-fine:gap-1`, giving the 4/4/12 rhythm visible at y=201/232/263/302.
direction: Size the field to its content — six characters, set large — so the box itself announces what is wanted, and put the button in immediate relation to it (beside it, or directly under it) with the lifetime hint moved out of the path between them.

where: `/kiosk` in the page intro and `/kiosk` in the 'Pair a kiosk' subtitle
finding: The same token is typeset two different ways eight lines apart: mono and ink-300 in the intro, plain body ink-500 in the card subtitle. The one that matters — the address the reader has to look at across the room — is the unmarked one, so the styling is doing the opposite of emphasis, and the inconsistency reads as two people having written the page.
evidence: `/kiosk` in the h1 subtitle; bare text '/kiosk' in the h2 subtitle immediately below.
direction: Give a literal path one treatment everywhere on the screen, and apply it in the instruction line at least as strongly as in the description.

where: the open account menu above the chip, read against the nav rail behind it
finding: The menu is a second navigation in a different alphabet, stacked directly under the first. The rail's five destinations are icon-plus-label on a 44px rhythm at x=25/51; the menu's items are label-only on a 36px rhythm at x=24, in a brighter ink. So 'Kiosk' — a page exactly like Events or Students — is the only destination in the app that arrives with no icon and no left-column alignment to the others. Inside the panel there is no differentiation at all: identity block, three destinations and a sign-out share one undifferentiated stack with identical padding, and the only thing marking the destructive item as a different species is that it is red — which also makes it the first thing the eye finds in the panel.
evidence: Rail items `flex min-h-11 items-center gap-3 px-3` with a glyph span; menu items `block px-3 py-2 text-ink-200` with no glyph and no separator before the `text-danger-400` Sign out.
direction: Either the menu's destinations adopt the rail's alphabet — same glyph column, same rhythm — so the list reads as one continuous set of places, or the menu stops pretending to be nav. Separate the identity block and the sign-out from the destinations so grouping, not colour, carries the difference; the red then stops being the loudest thing in a panel whose purpose is to get you to Kiosk.

where: the gcloud command block inside the amber panel
finding: The command is clipped hard at the panel's right edge, mid-token, with no fade, no wrap and no visible scroll affordance — the line simply stops inside the word. It reads as a rendering failure rather than a scrollable region, and it happens on a 1440px screen with ~290px of unused margin on either side of the column and half the viewport empty below, so the frame looks like it ran out of room when it plainly has not.
evidence: `<pre class="... overflow-x-auto ...">` truncating at x≈1380 on '…serviceAccountToken'; page content ends at y=820 with the whole lower band and both outer margins idle.
direction: Let the command wrap across lines rather than scroll, or give the clipped edge a visible end so the cut reads as a choice. Since a copy button already exists, wrapping costs nothing and removes a broken-looking edge.
